draft.title: Synaesthesia and spatial neglect
card: a condition in which one sense triggers another as well. For example, a person hears a sound and also sees a colour. The link is automatic and tends to stay the same over time.
a condition in which a person ignores one side of space, usually the side opposite to damage in the brain. It is often seen after a stroke.
In spatial neglect the eyes and the sensory pathways can work normally. The problem is in attending to and processing one side, so a person may eat only the food on one half of a plate.
Both conditions are distortions of perception. In synaesthesia there is an extra experience. In spatial neglect part of the world is not noticed.
draft.remember: Synaesthesia adds an extra sense experience. Spatial neglect leaves one side of space unnoticed.

a.q: Priya hears a trumpet and also sees a bright orange shape each time. Which term best describes this?
opts: Synaesthesia
Spatial neglect
Agnosia
A visual illusion
a.why: One sense (hearing) automatically triggers another (vision), which is synaesthesia. Spatial neglect is wrong because nothing is being ignored. Priya has an extra experience, not a missing one.
a.clue: Is something being added or ignored?

b.q: After a stroke, Tom shaves only the right half of his face and leaves the left half of his plate untouched. His eyes test as normal. What is the best explanation?
opts: He fails to attend to the left side of space
He cannot see anything on his left side
One of his senses is triggering another
He sees objects but cannot recognise them
b.why: Tom ignores one side of space even though his eyes work normally, which fits spatial neglect. Being unable to see the left side is tempting, but the eye tests rule it out. The problem is attention and processing, not vision.
b.clue: His eyes work normally, so look at attention.

b.best: He fails to attend to the left side of space

problems.detail: The clue 'look at attention' points straight at the only option containing 'attend', so a student can pick the answer without understanding spatial neglect.

'His eyes test as normal' does not strictly rule out being unable to see the left side, because a stroke can cause loss of half the visual field (hemianopia) even when the eyes are healthy. The why says the eye tests 'rule it out'. Wording such as 'his vision and visual field test as normal' would make the distractor clearly wrong.

check.summary: The facts on the card are correct and both questions have one clear answer. Question b's clue gives the answer away, and its 'eyes test as normal' wording does not fully rule out a stroke-related visual field loss.
